tips.title: Low means close to the machine
tips.body: **Low-level** does not mean simple or basic — it means **close to the hardware**. Machine code and assembly are low-level because they work in the processor's own instructions. High-level means close to the way **people** think.

tips.title: Three translators, two of them direct
tips.body: **Assemblers and compilers produce machine code directly.** **Interpreters do not** — they call machine code subroutines inside themselves to carry each statement out. That one distinction is stated in the specification and is worth a mark on its own.

tips.title: Assembly is 1:1, and that is the point
tips.body: Each line of assembly becomes **exactly one** machine code instruction. That is why an assembler is simple, and why assembly gives such precise control — and why 5 lines of assembly give 5 instructions, no more.

tips.title: Machine code is tied to its processor
tips.body: Each type of processor has **its own instruction set**, so machine code written for one will not run on a different family. High-level code can be recompiled for each — which is most of why people use it.

tips.title: Everything gets translated
tips.body: A processor executes **machine code only**. So all high-level **and** assembly code must be translated before it can run. Assembly is low-level but it still is not machine code.

why.matters:
A processor understands exactly one thing: **machine code**, in binary. Every language above that is a convenience for people, and everything written in one has to be translated before anything runs.

So this topic is about a trade that is made every time software is written. Closer to the hardware means more control and more speed, and code that works on one kind of processor only. Further away means readable, portable, far quicker to write — and one step removed from the machine. Almost everything is written high-level, and the exam wants the reason, not the fact.

examples.title: Why everything ends up as binary anyway
examples.body:
Nothing a processor is given is ever anything but machine code. Python, C# and assembly are all notations for people; each is turned into machine code before it can be executed, and only machine code needs no translation.

Worth being exact about two words that get swapped. **Machine code** is the binary the processor runs. **Assembly** is a human-readable version of it — mnemonics like `ADD` and `LDA`, one instruction each — and it still has to go through an assembler. Both are low-level, and they are not the same thing.

visual.alt: A table of three ways of writing a program: high-level languages and assembly both have to be translated first, and only machine code is what the processor actually runs

examples.title: Why almost nobody writes assembly any more
examples.body:
One line of a high-level language does the work of many machine instructions, and it says what it means. It also runs on any processor with a translator for it, while assembly is written for **one** instruction set and has to be rewritten for another.

Low-level has not gone away, though: where the exact instructions matter — a device driver, an embedded system with very little memory — the control is worth the cost. That is the shape of the answer an exam wants. Not *high-level is better*, but what each buys and what each costs.

visual.alt: A table comparing high-level and low-level languages: high-level is easier to write and portable between processors, low-level gives complete control of the hardware but must be rewritten for another instruction set

examples.title: Why an interpreter never leaves anything behind
examples.body:
A compiler translates the whole program in advance and produces machine code you can keep, run again, and give to somebody without the source. An interpreter translates and runs **one statement at a time**, and produces no machine code at all — nothing is kept, so it starts again from the source every run.

That last sentence is the detail that separates a full answer. It also explains the trade: interpreted code is slower to run and far quicker to test, because there is nothing to rebuild between one change and the next.

visual.alt: A table of the three translators: an assembler turns assembly into machine code, a compiler turns a high-level language into machine code, and an interpreter runs a high-level language a statement at a time and keeps nothing

steps.title: Two levels of language
steps.body:
**A processor understands one thing: machine code.** Everything else has to be translated into it before anything can run.

The specification divides languages into two **levels**.

**Low-level languages** work in the processor's own terms. There are two:

- **Machine code** — instructions **expressed in binary**, which the processor executes directly.
- **Assembly language** — the same instructions written with short mnemonics such as `LDA` or `ADD` instead of binary.

**High-level languages** — Python, C#, VB.NET — are written in terms closer to how **people** think about a problem. One line does the work of many machine instructions.

**"Low" does not mean simple.** It means **close to the hardware**. Low-level code is generally *harder* to write, not easier — you are managing the machine yourself.

**Machine code is specific to a processor.** Each type of processor has **its own instruction set**, so machine code written for one family will not run on another. A high-level program can be recompiled for each, which is a large part of why almost all software is written in high-level languages.

visuals.alt: A four-box card comparing machine code, assembly and high-level languages and what low-level means

check.prompt: What does it mean to call a language low-level?
options: It works closely with the hardware, in the processor's own terms
It is simpler and easier to learn than other languages
It can only be used to write very short programs
It runs more slowly than a high-level language
check.solution: **Low-level** means **close to the hardware**. It is usually *harder* to write than high-level code, not easier, and low-level code typically runs faster rather than slower.

steps.title: Machine code and assembly
steps.body:
**Both are low-level, and they are not the same thing.**

**Machine code** is **binary**. It is what the processor actually executes — no translation is needed, because this is the processor's own language.

**Assembly language** replaces those binary patterns with short **mnemonics** a person can read. `ADD` is easier to work with than a string of 0s and 1s, but the instructions are the same instructions.

**The key fact: assembly has a 1:1 correspondence with machine code.** Each line of assembly becomes **exactly one** machine code instruction. Write 5 lines, get 5 instructions.

That is what makes assembly low-level. A high-level language has no such relationship — one line of Python might become dozens of machine instructions, or none at all.

**Assembly still has to be translated.** It is not machine code; it is a readable way of writing machine code. The program that translates it is an **assembler**, and because of the 1:1 relationship an assembler has a simple job.

**Where assembly is actually used**, according to the specification:

- developing software for **embedded systems**
- **controlling specific hardware components**

Both are cases where the exact instructions and precise timing matter, and where memory is tight.

check.prompt: What is meant by saying assembly language has a 1:1 correspondence with machine code?
options: Each line of assembly becomes exactly one machine code instruction
Assembly and machine code are two names for the same thing
Assembly runs exactly as fast as machine code does
One assembly program produces one machine code file
check.solution: Each line of assembly is assembled into **one** machine code instruction. They are not the same thing — assembly still needs translating by an **assembler**.

steps.title: Why most programs are high-level
steps.body:
**The specification asks you to explain why most computer programs are written in high-level languages.** It comes down to a trade.

**Advantages of high-level:**

- **Easier and faster to write**, read and maintain — one line does the work of many.
- **Portable**: the same source can be recompiled for a **different processor**, where machine code cannot move at all.
- **Fewer mistakes**, and easier to find the ones you make.
- No need to know the processor's instruction set.

**Advantages of low-level:**

- **Direct control** of the hardware, down to individual instructions.
- Can be made to run **faster** and use **less memory**.
- Necessary where you must address particular hardware directly.

**Disadvantages of low-level:** hard to write, hard to read, very easy to get wrong, and **tied to one processor family** — move to a different processor and the work starts again.

**So the answer to "why high-level"** is that programmer time is expensive and computers are fast. For almost all software, being quick to write, easy to maintain and portable matters more than the last few percent of speed. Low-level is reserved for the cases where that trade goes the other way — **embedded systems** and **controlling specific hardware**.

props.title: Programmer time is expensive and computers are fast, which is why high-level usually wins

visuals.alt: A table comparing high-level and low-level languages across five criteria

check.prompt: Why are most computer programs written in high-level languages?
options: They are faster to write and can be recompiled for other processors
They always run faster than low-level programs
They do not need to be translated before running
They use less memory than low-level programs
check.solution: High-level code is **quicker to write and maintain** and is **portable** between processors. It usually runs **slower** and uses **more** memory than good low-level code, and it certainly still needs translating.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Say that an interpreter does not produce machine code.** This is the detail that separates a full answer. Assemblers and compilers translate **into machine code directly**; an interpreter **calls machine code subroutines within its own code** to carry each statement out. Most answers say an interpreter "translates line by line" and stop, which is true but is not the distinction the specification draws.

**Keep "low-level" and "simple" apart.** Low-level means **close to the hardware**. It is harder to write, not easier. Examiners see *low-level languages are easier because they are basic* regularly, and it is wrong twice over.

**Be precise about the 1:1 correspondence.** Each **line** of assembly becomes **one machine code instruction**. It does not mean assembly *is* machine code — assembly still needs an assembler.

**Explain portability properly.** Machine code is tied to a processor because **each type of processor has its own instruction set**. High-level code is portable not because it runs anywhere as-is, but because it can be **recompiled** for each target. That distinction is worth making.

**Give the real reason high-level dominates.** Programmer time is expensive and computers are fast, so being quick to write, easy to maintain and portable beats the last few percent of performance for almost all software. Low-level survives exactly where that trade reverses — **embedded systems** and **controlling specific hardware**.

**Match the translator to the stage.** An **interpreter** suits development and debugging, because it runs up to the error and stops there. A **compiler** suits shipping, because the customer gets an executable that runs without a translator present and runs faster. Saying *when* as well as *what* is what the specification asks for.

**Remember assembly is still translated.** It is low-level, but it is not machine code. Only machine code runs untranslated.

steps.body:

- **Low-level** means **close to the hardware**, not simple.
- The two low-level languages are **machine code** and **assembly**.
- **Machine code** is expressed in **binary** and runs directly.
- **Assembly** uses **mnemonics** and has a **1:1 correspondence** with machine code.
- One line of assembly becomes **exactly one** machine code instruction.
- Assembly is used for **embedded systems** and **controlling specific hardware**.
- All **high-level and assembly** code must be **translated**.
- Each processor type has **its own instruction set**, so machine code is not portable.
- High-level code is **portable** because it can be **recompiled**.
- High-level: easier, faster to write, portable, fewer errors.
- Low-level: direct hardware control, can be faster and smaller.
- Three translators: **assembler**, **compiler**, **interpreter**.
- **Assemblers and compilers** produce machine code **directly**; **interpreters do not**.
- A **compiler** translates everything first; an **interpreter** translates and runs a line at a time.

questions.prompt: Explain the differences between low-level and high-level languages, and explain why most computer programs are written in high-level languages.
questions.solution:
**Low-level languages** work in the processor's own terms — "low" refers to the **distance from the hardware**, not to difficulty. There are two. **Machine code** is expressed in **binary** and is executed directly by the processor with no translation. **Assembly language** writes the same instructions using short **mnemonics** such as `ADD` or `LDA`, and has a **1:1 correspondence** with machine code: each line becomes **exactly one** machine code instruction. Assembly is still not machine code, so it must be translated by an **assembler**.

**High-level languages** — Python, C#, VB.NET — are written in terms much closer to how a person thinks about the problem. There is no 1:1 relationship: a single high-level line may become dozens of machine instructions. High-level code must also be translated, by a **compiler** or an **interpreter**.

**The differences that matter** follow from this. Low-level code gives **direct, precise control** of the hardware and can be made to run **faster** and in **less memory**. Against that, it is **difficult to write and read**, easy to get wrong, and **tied to one processor family**, because each type of processor has **its own instruction set**.

High-level code is **much faster to write**, easier to read and maintain, and produces fewer errors. It is also **portable**, though in a specific sense worth stating carefully: the **source code** can be **recompiled** for a different processor. The compiled machine code itself is no more portable than any other machine code.

**Most programs are written in high-level languages** because of how that trade falls in practice. Programmer time is expensive and computers are fast, so for almost all software, being quick to write, easy to maintain and portable is worth far more than the last few percent of speed or memory. A large program would be impractical to write and maintain in assembly at all.

Low-level languages survive precisely where the trade reverses. The specification names **developing software for embedded systems** and **controlling specific hardware components** — situations where memory is tight, exact timing matters, and particular hardware must be addressed directly.

questions.prompt: Describe the three types of translator, explain how they differ, and explain which would be appropriate at different stages of developing and releasing a program.
questions.solution:
All code written in a **high-level or assembly** language must be translated, because a processor executes **machine code** only. The specification names **three** types of translator.

An **assembler** translates **assembly language** into machine code. Because of the **1:1 correspondence**, each line of assembly becomes exactly one machine code instruction, which makes the assembler's job a straightforward substitution.

A **compiler** translates a **high-level** program into machine code, translating **the whole program before it runs**. The result is an executable file which then runs on its own, with no translator present.

An **interpreter** also takes a **high-level** program, but translates and executes it **one line at a time**, and must be present every time the program runs.

**The distinction the specification draws** is about what each **produces**. Assemblers and compilers **translate their input into machine code directly**. An interpreter **does not generate machine code directly** — it calls appropriate **machine code subroutines within its own code** to carry out each statement. Saying only that an interpreter "works line by line" leaves this out, and it is the part that separates a full answer.

The practical consequences follow. A **compiled** program runs **faster**, because translation has already happened and is not repeated, and it can be distributed without the source or a translator. An **interpreted** program starts running immediately with no compilation step, and stops **at** the line that fails.

**Applied to the stages of a project:**

While **developing and debugging**, an **interpreter** suits the work well. It runs up to the failing line and stops there, so the error is located immediately, and a small change can be tried straight away without waiting for a full recompilation. Over many short edit-and-test cycles that saves a great deal of time.

When **releasing to customers**, a **compiler** is the right choice. Customers get an executable that runs **faster** and needs **no translator installed**, and the source code is not distributed with it. The one-off cost of compiling is paid by the developer rather than by every user on every run.

An **assembler** would only be involved if part of the system — a device driver or an embedded component — had been written in assembly for direct hardware control.

examinerErrors: Describing an interpreter only as "translating line by line".
Saying low-level languages are easier because they are simpler.
Treating assembly language as though it were machine code.
Forgetting that assembly must be translated by an assembler.
Claiming compiled machine code runs on any processor.
Naming a translator without saying when it would be used.
Saying high-level programs run faster than low-level ones.
Giving "it is easier" as the whole reason high-level dominates.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer states that an **interpreter does not generate machine code directly**, and that assemblers and compilers do. It treats **low-level** as meaning close to the hardware, and therefore **harder**, not simpler. It is exact about the **1:1 correspondence** — one line, one instruction — while noting assembly still needs an assembler. It explains portability as the **source** being **recompiled** rather than machine code running anywhere, and it justifies high-level dominance by the real trade: **programmer time against a few percent of speed**, with low-level kept for **embedded systems and hardware control** where that trade reverses.
